title: OCC releases new guidance for reviewing AI in banks
excerpt: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has issued the “ OCC Supervisory Framework for Bank Use of Super Intelligence ” to guide examiners assessing AI use at U. S. national banks and other institutions it regulates. The guidance tells examiners to consider what an AI system can do, the consequences if it fails and how much human oversight it receives. The framework does not introduce new requirements for banks. Instead, it helps examiners assess AI-related risks within existing supervisory practices, with greater attention to systems that can make decisions or take actions without human intervention. The OCC’s accompanying bulletin explicitly says banks are not expected to use the framework to assess their own AI operations. The guidance follows an April revision to federal banking regulators’ model-risk management guidance, which excluded generative and agentic AI models from its scope. The OCC’s new framework gives its examiners a separate resource for assessing risks involving those technologies. The OCC’s use of “super intelligence” follows a September executive order directing federal agencies to adopt the term in place of AI, without changing the technologies covered by the existing statutory definition. Examiners should assess AI-related risks within existing categories, including operational, credit and compliance risk. Banks are not required to establish a separate AI risk appetite. Consequences over sophistication. The framework’s central distinction is between a system’s sophistication and the harm it could cause. A simple rules-based agent authorized to initiate transactions could pose greater risk than a sophisticated AI model used only to draft internal documents, it says. The difference lies in the authority granted to the system and the consequences of a mistake. The OCC illustrates its approach through four risk tiers. Autonomous payment agents, real-time credit decisions and systems that release fraud holds fall into the highest-risk tier. The lowest tier covers fully human-controlled internal productivity tools with no customer or financial data exposure or direct action. The tiers are examples for examiners, not mandatory classifications for banks. Human oversight and intervention. The OCC distinguishes approval before an AI action from ongoing monitoring with the ability to intervene. The framework says reviewers may need sufficient expertise, information and authority to reject or stop an AI action. Simply requiring someone to approve an output may offer little protection if that person cannot assess it properly. Bulk approvals can further weaken the review process. For autonomous agents, the framework goes beyond reviewing individual decisions. An agent can continue operating even while taking harmful actions, making it important to consider how failures are detected and contained. For higher-risk uses, the OCC discusses monitoring, intervention and mechanisms to suspend or shut down an agent. Vendor AI remains the bank’s responsibility. The OCC says responsibility for managing AI-related risks generally remains with the bank, even when outside providers develop, host or operate the technology. In assessing third-party AI risks, the framework points to vendor notifications, contractual liability and controls over what provider-operated agents can access and do within bank systems. Banks may require notice when suppliers add AI features or change underlying models, while contracts may address responsibility for model-related errors and losses. The framework also applies to community banks, although the OCC says examiners should adjust their reviews to each institution’s size, complexity and risk profile.

title: Banks Face Agentic AI’s Twin Tests: Customer Authority and Internal Costs
excerpt: Banks Face Agentic AI’s Twin Tests: Customer Authority and Internal Costs. By PYMNTS | November 13, 2026. |. Banks face a two-sided challenge as artificial intelligence (AI) agents move from answering questions to taking action. On one side is the need to control the legal risks when customers delegate financial decisions; on the other is the need to contain the costs of deploying agents themselves. A WilmerHale client alert and a Reuters report on McKinsey’s Global Banking Annual Review describe pressures that could reshape banks’ controls and economics. Customer agents may test established concepts of consent and accountability. Internally, agents’ interactions can generate computing bills that undermine expected savings. The immediate compliance issue is determining whose instructions a bank is executing. WilmerHale’s analysis, focused on the U. K. Financial Conduct Authority framework, distinguishes authenticating an agent from establishing its authority. Software may legitimately access an account yet make a transfer or investment outside the limits its customer intended. Under the U. K. Payment Services Regulations, payment authorization depends on payer consent through a procedure agreed with the provider. Strong customer authentication is a separate requirement. Establishing a connection between customer and agent does not necessarily settle whether a particular transaction was authorized. An instruction to manage cash efficiently, for example, could leave uncertainty over permitted amounts, counterparties or products. Banks need to consider how authority is established, restricted and withdrawn, and when customers must approve further action. Those concerns help explain the industry’s caution. Reuters reported that most banks currently block external agents from authorizing transactions within their systems, limiting their impact on deposits and profits. Demand nevertheless appears substantial. McKinsey surveyed 46,000 retail banking customers worldwide. Among AI users, 72% said they would allow a banking agent to perform one financial task, although they would cap autonomous approvals at $500. The consultancy expects widespread customer use of agents within three years. Delegation also complicates financial crime monitoring. WilmerHale describes an agent choosing payment methods, currencies or intermediaries to complete a supplier payment quickly and cheaply. Individually understandable actions could collectively produce unusual activity. An agent might also respond to a blocked transaction by seeking another route. Existing anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations still apply. The operational challenge is distinguishing legitimate automated behavior from fraud or evasion, and deciding when repeated activity requires human scrutiny. Evidence becomes especially important when a customer disputes a transaction. Ordinary records may show what the bank received and executed without establishing whether the agent followed its instructions. Relevant material could include permissions, customer communications and action histories. WilmerHale cautions that banks should consider what evidence they need to accept agent-initiated transactions, even where responsibility for creating those records lies elsewhere. Banks face a different control problem with their own agents in the form of unpredictable consumption of tokens, the units underlying AI processing charges. Reuters reported McKinsey’s warning that token spending could easily reach 20% of banks’ total labor costs. Some banks have assigned spending oversight to teams called AI FinOps. Earlier approaches directed employees to use different models according to query complexity. Agent-to-agent communication makes that approach less effective because usage accumulates across interactions. title: Hybrid stacking and logistic regression meta-model for credit card fraud detection using SMOTE and multiple machine learning algorithms
excerpt: Hybrid stacking and logistic regression meta-model for credit card fraud detection using SMOTE and multiple machine learning algorithms. Article. Open access. Published: 13 November 2026. Volume 16 , article number 37974 ( 2026 ). Cite this article. You have full access to this open access article. Download PDF. View saved research. Hybrid stacking and logistic regression meta-model for credit card fraud detection using SMOTE and multiple machine learning algorithms. Download PDF. Abstract. This study presents a stacking ensemble framework for credit card fraud detection on the imbalanced Kaggle dataset, using SMOTE to address class imbalance. Base classifiers (RF, SVM, KNN, NB, GB, LR) are evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, with RF and KNN emerging as the strongest learners, reaching 97% recall and 0. 98 F1-score after SMOTE. The final ensemble employs RF and KNN as base learners with Logistic Regression as the meta-classifier, and pairwise prediction correlations (r ≈ 0. 34 for RF–KNN vs. r ≈ 0. 81 for RF–GB) confirm that RF and KNN form a more diverse and complementary pair. A refined stacked hybrid using RF–KNN–GB with meta-features and original data achieves the best trade-off for fraud and intrusion detection, obtaining 0. 975 recall with only one false positive, 0. 9968 precision, 0. 986 F1-score, and accuracy of 0. 9997, outperforming existing hybrid methods. These findings demonstrate that carefully designed ensembles and feature engineering can deliver robust fraud detection on highly imbalanced data, surpassing individual models and reported. title: Thousands of AI agents, but how much control do banks really have?

excerpt: detail. * It has been translated using AI. "AI kill switch alone is not enough. You should have a system for people to take over the work. ". Suppose Bank A entrusted most of the loan screening tasks to artificial intelligence (AI). As AI replaced the work that 100 employees were doing, the number of people in charge decreased to 20. The pace of screening has accelerated and labor costs have been reduced. However, one day, AI began to produce false screening results. The bank turned off the AI to prevent the damage. The question is next. With the remaining 20 employees, it is difficult to handle the rush of loan applications. Employees' screening ability has also declined because they have been entrusted with AI for a long time. Although AI's errors have been prevented, the banking business is on the verge of being paralyzed. Global market research firm Gartner pointed to the situation that can occur when AI stops as a new management risk. The bank case is a hypothetical situation, but it illustrates the risk of AI dependence that Gartner warned about. Gartner pointed out in a recently released 'AI Kill Switch is not enough: Can a company continue to operate even if AI stops?' "The biggest risk to AI is not to lose control of it, but to lose the ability to operate without it. ". As companies speed up the introduction of AI, the risk of business interruption is also increasing. In a situation where AI consults customers, analyzes data, and even replaces decision-making, if one AI system stops, the core work of the company can also be stopped. In fact, in Korea, insurance company B has significantly reduced the existing counseling staff by upgrading AI chatbots for non-face-to-face channel sales. If AI causes problems, it can be overloaded with work. Until now, companies have focused on "Kill Switch," which stops AI when it causes errors or goes out of control. It is a device that immediately stops dangerous AI, such as an emergency brake of a car. But Gartner pointed out that this is not enough. This is because even if AI is stopped, the work that the system was handling will not be restored by itself. Accordingly, Gartner's solution is "Continuity Switch. " It refers to an emergency operating system that prepares employees or other systems to take over their work even if AI stops. In other words, it is necessary to have a device that stops AI and a device that continues to work together. Especially noteworthy is a person's ability to work. The longer AI takes over for work, the weaker the ability of employees to handle work themselves. It is a warning that employees may find it difficult to work without AI as the experience and expertise accumulated in companies shift to AI systems. Dependence on external AI companies was also cited as a risk factor. This is because companies that entrust core tasks to a specific AI model can be hit just by the company suspending its service or changing the terms of the contract. This means that even if there is no problem with the company's internal system, work can be stopped by decisions made by external companies. Gartner highlighted the continuity switch, citing examples in which AI's wrong answers harmed companies. Air Canada's Customer Counseling Chatbot misguided special airfare and refund regulations following family deaths, resulting in legal liability and reputational damage to the company. Gartner explained that in this case, AI functions in question should be limited, but counselors should continue to respond to customers. Gartner suggested that companies should first understand the core tasks entrusted to AI and check the damage that will occur in the event of AI interruption. He added that employees should be trained to maintain their ability to handle tasks directly and that simulation training assuming AI failures should be conducted regularly. The greater the dependence on AI, the more prepared it is to be able to withstand it without AI. #. Most Read News. 1. Following Alice
